newsitem.title: FRANCE: French opposition sees austerity behind election.
newsitem.headline: French opposition sees austerity behind election.

text.p: French opposition parties accused President Jacques Chirac on Monday of planning new austerity behind a snap election while Chirac's centre-right allies hailed the vote as a bold gamble to aid European integration.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin said the government was preparing "a new step towards a harsh capitalism" in the belief it could win the National Assembly election on May 25 and June 1, more than nine months ahead of schedule.
Chirac, announcing the vote on Monday night, said it was needed to help France regain vigour and join a single European currency in 1999 from a position of strength.

Jospin, defeated by Chirac in the 1995 presidential election, said Chirac was seeking to pre-empt the failure of his economic policies, prepare tougher austerity and head off sleaze scandals threatening members of the centre-right coalition.
Extreme right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen blasted the election, as "an electoral hold-up" and a "shameful swindle".
He said it robbed voters of the chance of judging the government in 1998 after what he predicted would be a year of austerity, high taxes and job losses.

But members of the centre-right coalition approved Chirac's bid to ensure the campaign will not be overshadowed by wrangling in the European Union in early 1998 over which nations qualify for the single currency.
"This decision is legitimate, necessary, and in line with the good exercise of democracy," said Francois Leotard, head of the Union for French Democracy (UDF), the junior partner in the coalition.
"The battle for employment supposes rapid decisions, notably for lower charges...and lower taxes," he said. Unemployment is at a record high of 12.8 percent.
Michel Pericard, parliamentary floor leader of the Rally for the Republic Party (RPR) founded by Chirac, said RPR deputies "overwhelmingly approved" Chirac's decision.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said the original electoral timetable was a recipe for political paralysis in France at a crucial time for Europe. "To get the country moving, the best way is to return to the people," he said.

Communist leader Robert Hue said the French economy was "disastrous...but he wants to go even further. We're being told of a super austerity...The dissolution is taking place because a terrible new turn of the screws is being prepared."
Former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius accused Chirac of seeking a blank cheque from voters before the effects of a new bout of austerity were felt.
"The president is telling us: if you vote for the parties on the right, the euro will happen," he said.
"It's more complicated than that. We favour the construction of Europe but we don't want it to the detriment of economic activity, to the detriment of France."
